narrative:
The law school denied your application because the model estimated an 83% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. In practical terms, the model placed you in a high-risk group: among applicants with a similar profile, most were predicted to fail rather than pass. This is a forecast, not a judgment of your ability, but it was strong enough to drive the admission decision.

The strongest factor was your LSAT score of 24, well below the average of 37.18 among accepted students. This was the single most influential feature and pushed the prediction toward failure. The next most important factor was your first-year class-rank decile of 5, below the accepted-student average of 6; that also pushed toward failure, though less strongly. Your third-year decile of 4, compared with an average of 5.79, was the third most important factor and likewise increased the predicted risk. These academic indicators together outweighed other information such as family income and full-time status.

To strengthen a future application, focus on the areas the model weighted most: prepare for a higher LSAT score, and address any academic weaknesses reflected in your class-rank history through additional coursework, recommendations, or a clear explanation of improvement. Consider applying after demonstrating stronger bar-readiness, and ask an admissions advisor what evidence would best offset this prediction.
